claim: Ventral stress fibers are the most prominent actomyosin bundles in cells.
source: The most prominent actomyosin bundles, ventral stress fibers, are generated through coalescence of pre-existing stress fiber precursors.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract of the manuscript.

claim: Ventral stress fibers are generated through coalescence of pre-existing stress fiber precursors.
source: The most prominent actomyosin bundles, ventral stress fibers, are generated through coalescence of pre-existing stress fiber precursors.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Cortical stress fibers are embedded in the cell cortex.
source: These structures, which we named cortical stress fibers, are embedded in the cell cortex and assemble preferentially underneath the nucleus.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by imaging data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Cortical stress fibers assemble preferentially underneath the nucleus.
source: These structures, which we named cortical stress fibers, are embedded in the cell cortex and assemble preferentially underneath the nucleus.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and quantified in Figure 3B showing ~80% of cortical stress fibers assembled underneath the nucleus.

claim: Non-muscle myosin II pulses orchestrate the reorganization of cortical actin meshwork into regular bundles during cortical stress fiber assembly.
source: In this process, non-muscle myosin II pulses orchestrate the reorganization of cortical actin meshwork into regular bundles, which promote reinforcement of nascent focal adhesions, and subsequent stabilization of the cortical stress fibers.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through live-cell imaging in Figures 3D and 4A.

claim: Cortical stress fiber assembly promotes reinforcement of nascent focal adhesions.
source: In this process, non-muscle myosin II pulses orchestrate the reorganization of cortical actin meshwork into regular bundles, which promote reinforcement of nascent focal adhesions, and subsequent stabilization of the cortical stress fibers.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in time-lapse imaging data in Figures 2A, 2B, and 4A.

claim: Cortical stress fibers can be generated de novo from the actin cortex without requirement of pre-existing actomyosin bundles.
source: We report that stress fibers can also form without requirement of pre-existing actomyosin bundles.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through time-lapse imaging in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: Stochastic myosin pulses play a role in the assembly of functional actomyosin bundles.
source: These results identify a new mechanism by which stress fibers can be generated de novo from the actin cortex and establish role for stochastic myosin pulses in the assembly of functional actomyosin bundles.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by imaging data in Figures 3D and 4A-C.

claim: Cell migration, morphogenesis, and adhesion depend on contractile networks composed of actin and non-muscle myosin II filaments.
source: Cell migration, morphogenesis, and adhesion depend on contractile networks composed of actin and non-muscle myosin II (NMII) filaments.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established scientific knowledge.

claim: Forces in actomyosin structures are generated through sliding of bipolar NMII filaments along actin.
source: The forces in these structures are generated through sliding of bipolar NMII filaments along actin.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge about actomyosin contractility.

claim: Assembly and contractility of actomyosin arrays are controlled by Rho-family GTPases, kinase-phosphatase pathways, and Ca2+ influxes.
source: Assembly and contractility of these actomyosin arrays are controlled by upstream signals including Rho-family GTPases, kinase-phosphatase pathways, and Ca2+ influxes (Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2009; Prager-Khoutorsky et al., 2011; Tojkander et al., 2015; Tojkander et al., 2018; Burridge and Guilluy, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple supporting citations.

claim: The actin cortex is a thin meshwork beneath the plasma membrane composed of actin filaments, NMII filaments, and associated proteins.
source: Beneath the plasma membrane of animal cells lies a thin meshwork that is composed of actin filaments, NMII filaments, and associated proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge about cell structure.

claim: The actin cortex contributes to morphogenesis of interphase cells and drives cell rounding during cytokinesis.
source: This structure, the actin cortex, contributes to morphogenesis of interphase cells, and drives cell rounding during cytokinesis (Bray and White, 1988; Chugh and Paluch, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: In human cells, the assembly of actin cortex depends on both formins and the Arp2/3 complex.
source: In human cells, the assembly of actin cortex depends on both formins and the Arp2/3 complex (Bovellan et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2017; Cao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: ERM-family proteins link the cortical actin meshwork to the plasma membrane in interphase cells and during mitosis.
source: Ezrin, radixin, moesin (ERM)-family proteins link the cortical actin meshwork to the plasma membrane in interphase cells and during mitosis (Bretscher et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Cortical actin meshwork is constantly under isotropic tension due to intracellular hydrostatic pressure and NMII-generated contractile forces.
source: Cortical actin meshwork is constantly under isotropic tension due to intracellular hydrostatic pressure and NMII-generated contractile forces to the actin cortex, and this can lead to formation of membrane blebs through local detachment of the actin cortex from the plasma membrane (Charras and Paluch, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Stress fibers are thick, contractile actin bundles that often connect to focal adhesions at their ends.
source: These thick, contractile actin bundles often connect to focal adhesions at their ends, and they are especially prominent in cells plated on stiff matrix or when external force is applied to the cells.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge about stress fibers.

claim: Stress fibers are especially prominent in cells plated on stiff matrix or when external force is applied to the cells.
source: These thick, contractile actin bundles often connect to focal adhesions at their ends, and they are especially prominent in cells plated on stiff matrix or when external force is applied to the cells.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge.

claim: Stress fibers, together with focal adhesions, constitute a major mechanosensitive machinery in cells.
source: Thus, stress fibers, together with focal adhesions, constitute a major mechanosensitive machinery in cells (Tojkander et al., 2012; Livne and Geiger, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Stress fibers contribute to cell morphogenesis and tail retraction during migration.
source: Apart from adhesion and mechanosensing, stress fibers contribute to cell morphogenesis and tail retraction during migration.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge.

claim: Stress fibers serve as precursors for sarcomeres during cardiomyocyte myofibrillogenesis.
source: Stress fibers also serve as precursors for sarcomeres during cardiomyocyte myofibrillogenesis (Fenix et al., 2018), and stress fiber-like actomyosin bundles contribute to interactions of epithelial cells with their neighbors and with basal lamina (Yamada and Nelson, 2007; Munjal et al., 2015; López-Gay et al., 2020; Rajakylä et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Ventral stress fibers are thick actomyosin bundles that are connected from their both ends to focal adhesions at the bottom of the cell.
source: Ventral stress fibers are thick actomyosin bundles that are connected from their both ends to focal adhesions at the bottom of the cell.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge about stress fiber classification.

claim: The central regions of ventral stress fibers often rise toward the dorsal surface of cell.
source: Despite their name, the central regions of ventral stress fibers often rise toward the dorsal surface of cell (Naumanen et al., 2008; Burnette et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: In many cell types, ventral stress fibers associate with each other to form a complex, mechanically interconnected network.
source: In many cell types, ventral stress fibers associate with each other to form a complex, mechanically interconnected network (Xu et al., 2012; Kassianidou et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Dorsal stress fibers are non-contractile actin filament bundles that are generated at the cell front through formin- and VASP-mediated actin filament assembly at focal adhesions.
source: Dorsal stress fibers (also known as radial fibers) are non-contractile actin filament bundles that are generated at the cell front through formin- and VASP-mediated actin filament assembly at focal adhesions (Hotulainen and Lappalainen, 2006; Tee et al., 2015; Tojkander et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Transverse arcs are thin, contractile actomyosin bundles, arising through NMII-promoted condensing of the lamellipodial actin network at the cell edge.
source: Transverse arcs, on the other hand, are thin, contractile actomyosin bundles, arising through NMII-promoted condensing of the lamellipodial actin network at the cell edge (Hotulainen and Lappalainen, 2006; Burnette et al., 2011; Tojkander et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Transverse arcs undergo retrograde flow toward the cell center following their appearance.
source: Following their appearance, transverse arcs undergo retrograde flow toward the cell center, fuse with each other into thicker bundles, and become more contractile due to concatenation and persistent expansion of NMII filaments into stacks (Tojkander et al., 2015; Fenix et al., 2016; Beach et al., 2017; Hu et al., 2017; Jiu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Transverse arcs fuse with each other into thicker bundles.
source: Following their appearance, transverse arcs undergo retrograde flow toward the cell center, fuse with each other into thicker bundles, and become more contractile due to concatenation and persistent expansion of NMII filaments into stacks (Tojkander et al., 2015; Fenix et al., 2016; Beach et al., 2017; Hu et al., 2017; Jiu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Transverse arcs become more contractile due to concatenation and persistent expansion of NMII filaments into stacks.
source: Following their appearance, transverse arcs undergo retrograde flow toward the cell center, fuse with each other into thicker bundles, and become more contractile due to concatenation and persistent expansion of NMII filaments into stacks (Tojkander et al., 2015; Fenix et al., 2016; Beach et al., 2017; Hu et al., 2017; Jiu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Transverse arcs are not directly linked to focal adhesions.
source: Although transverse arcs are not directly linked to focal adhesions, they associate with focal adhesion-connected dorsal stress fibers (Burnette et al., 2014; Senger et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Transverse arcs associate with focal adhesion-connected dorsal stress fibers.
source: Although transverse arcs are not directly linked to focal adhesions, they associate with focal adhesion-connected dorsal stress fibers (Burnette et al., 2014; Senger et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Ventral stress fibers can be generated from the transverse arc and dorsal stress fiber network through a complex process.
source: Ventral stress fibers can be generated from the transverse arc and dorsal stress fiber network through a complex process that involves both mechanosensitive regulation of actin filament assembly at focal adhesions, as well as inhibition of actin disassembly within the stress fiber network (Hayakawa et al., 2011; Tojkander et al., 2015; Tojkander et al., 2018; Lee and Kumar, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Pre-existing ventral stress fibers can undergo 'splitting' to generate new, adjacent ventral stress fibers.
source: Moreover, pre-existing ventral stress fibers can undergo 'splitting' to generate new, adjacent ventral stress fibers (Young and Higgs, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: U2OS and MEF cells exhibit thin and relatively short actomyosin bundles that are connected to small focal adhesions at their both ends.
source: In addition to thick ventral stress fibers that connect focal adhesions located at the opposite sides of the cell, both cell types exhibited thin and relatively short actomyosin bundles that were connected to small focal adhesions at their both ends.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Thin actomyosin bundles reside at the immediate vicinity of the ventral cortex of the cell.
source: As illustrated by the temporal-color coded 3D-SIM projections of F-actin, these thin actomyosin bundles reside at the immediate vicinity of the ventral cortex of the cell (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, white arrows), whereas typical ventral stress fibers (Burnette et al., 2014; Tojkander et al., 2015) rise toward the dorsal surface from the middle of the bundle (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; red arrows).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to imaging data in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Typical ventral stress fibers rise toward the dorsal surface from the middle of the bundle.
source: As illustrated by the temporal-color coded 3D-SIM projections of F-actin, these thin actomyosin bundles reside at the immediate vicinity of the ventral cortex of the cell (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, white arrows), whereas typical ventral stress fibers (Burnette et al., 2014; Tojkander et al., 2015) rise toward the dorsal surface from the middle of the bundle (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; red arrows).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to imaging data and supporting citations.

claim: NMII filaments display a bipolar arrangement in cortical stress fibers.
source: Similar to the ventral stress fibers, NMII filaments displayed a bipolar arrangement in the small, basally located cortical stress fibers (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: NMII does not assemble into stacks in cortical stress fibers.
source: However, NMII did not appear to assemble into stacks, and the periodic pattern of actin filament cross-linking protein α-actinin was less regular in cortical stress fibers compared to transverse arcs and ventral stress fibers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The periodic pattern of α-actinin is less regular in cortical stress fibers compared to transverse arcs and ventral stress fibers.
source: However, NMII did not appear to assemble into stacks, and the periodic pattern of actin filament cross-linking protein α-actinin was less regular in cortical stress fibers compared to transverse arcs and ventral stress fibers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The forces exerted by cortical stress fibers to the ECM are much smaller compared to typical ventral stress fibers.
source: Moreover, the forces exerted by cortical stress fibers to the ECM were much smaller compared to typical ventral stress fibers (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to traction force microscopy data in Figure 1C.

claim: Cortical stress fibers are most prevalently observed in cells migrating on fibronectin.
source: Although cortical stress fibers were able to form also on laminin and collagen, they were most prevalently observed in cells migrating on fibronectin (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to imaging data in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Cortical stress fibers can form on laminin and collagen.
source: Although cortical stress fibers were able to form also on laminin and collagen, they were most prevalently observed in cells migrating on fibronectin (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to imaging data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The adhesions at the ends of cortical stress fibers contain Y118-phospho(p)-paxillin.
source: Moreover, the adhesions at the ends of cortical stress fibers contained Y118-phospho(p)-paxillin, indicating that they were not associated with fibrillar adhesions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to imaging data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The adhesions at the ends of cortical stress fibers are not associated with fibrillar adhesions.
source: Moreover, the adhesions at the ends of cortical stress fibers contained Y118-phospho(p)-paxillin, indicating that they were not associated with fibrillar adhesions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to imaging data and inferred from the presence of Y118-phospho(p)-paxillin.

claim: The molecular composition of cortical stress fibers closely resembles that of ventral stress fibers.
source: Taken together, the molecular composition of cortical stress fibers closely resembles the one of ventral stress fibers, but they are typically much smaller, localize consistently at the ventral actin cortex, and exert only weak traction forces.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary of the observations from Figure 1 and related supplementary figures.

claim: Cortical stress fibers are typically much smaller than ventral stress fibers.
source: Taken together, the molecular composition of cortical stress fibers closely resembles the one of ventral stress fibers, but they are typically much smaller, localize consistently at the ventral actin cortex, and exert only weak traction forces.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary of observations from imaging data.

claim: Cortical stress fibers localize consistently at the ventral actin cortex.
source: Taken together, the molecular composition of cortical stress fibers closely resembles the one of ventral stress fibers, but they are typically much smaller, localize consistently at the ventral actin cortex, and exert only weak traction forces.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary of observations from imaging data.

claim: Cortical stress fibers exert only weak traction forces.
source: Taken together, the molecular composition of cortical stress fibers closely resembles the one of ventral stress fibers, but they are typically much smaller, localize consistently at the ventral actin cortex, and exert only weak traction forces.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary of traction force microscopy data from Figure 1C.

claim: Cortical stress fibers emerge de novo from the ventral actin cortex without involvement of any pre-existing stress fiber precursors.
source: Surprisingly, these experiments revealed that cortical stress fibers emerged de novo from the ventral actin cortex, without involvement of any pre-existing stress fiber precursors (Figure 2A and B and Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to time-lapse imaging data in Figure 2A and B and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: During cortical stress fiber assembly, actin filaments of the cell cortex reorganize into thicker bundles.
source: In this process, actin filaments of the cell cortex reorganized into thicker bundles (Figure 2A and B, blue arrows) and this was followed by growth of nascent, initially barely visible, vinculin-positive adhesions at the both ends of the bundle (Figure 2A and B, orange arrows).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to time-lapse imaging data in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Actin filament bundling during cortical stress fiber assembly is followed by growth of nascent vinculin-positive adhesions at both ends of the bundle.
source: In this process, actin filaments of the cell cortex reorganized into thicker bundles (Figure 2A and B, blue arrows) and this was followed by growth of nascent, initially barely visible, vinculin-positive adhesions at the both ends of the bundle (Figure 2A and B, orange arrows).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to time-lapse imaging data in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Unlike dorsal stress fibers, cortical stress fibers do not elongate through actin polymerization from adhesions.
source: This provides evidence that, unlike dorsal stress fibers, cortical stress fibers do not elongate from adhesions at their ends (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to photoactivation experiments in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Photoactivated regions in dorsal stress fibers display a centripetal movement with a typical rate of ~0.3 µm/min.
source: Whereas the photoactivated regions in dorsal stress fibers displayed a centripetal movement with a typical rate of ~0.3 µm/min, the photoactivated regions in cortical stress fibers were nearly immobile.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to photoactivation experiments in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Photoactivated regions in cortical stress fibers are nearly immobile.
source: Whereas the photoactivated regions in dorsal stress fibers displayed a centripetal movement with a typical rate of ~0.3 µm/min, the photoactivated regions in cortical stress fibers were nearly immobile.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to photoactivation experiments in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Cortical stress fibers are typically very dynamic with relatively short half-life (~25 min).
source: Live-cell imaging experiments also demonstrated that cortical stress fibers are typically very dynamic with relatively short half-life (~25 min).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on live-cell imaging experiments.

claim: The half-life of cortical stress fibers is highly variable from few minutes to more than 1.5 hr.
source: However, it is important to note that the half-life of cortical stress fibers was highly variable from few minutes to more than 1.5 hr.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on live-cell imaging experiments.

claim: Cortical stress fibers often associate dynamically with each other.
source: Moreover, cortical stress fibers often associated dynamically with each other, and they could also arise via various intermediate assembly states (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and Video 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to imaging data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and Video 3.

claim: Cortical stress fibers can arise via various intermediate assembly states.
source: Moreover, cortical stress fibers often associated dynamically with each other, and they could also arise via various intermediate assembly states (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and Video 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to imaging data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and Video 3.

claim: Cortical stress fibers are enriched at the rear of migrating cells.
source: Cortical stress fibers were enriched at the rear of migrating cells and were typically located either underneath or close to the nucleus (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to imaging data in Figure 1.

claim: Cortical stress fibers are typically located either underneath or close to the nucleus.
source: Cortical stress fibers were enriched at the rear of migrating cells and were typically located either underneath or close to the nucleus (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to imaging data in Figure 1.

claim: The nucleus undergoes NMII-dependent translocation as the cell moves forward.
source: Nucleus is a relatively bulky organelle, localized behind the lamella at the cell rear in polarized mesenchymal cells, and it undergoes NMII-dependent translocation as the cell moves forward (Wu et al., 2014; Thomas et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: The assembly of cortical stress fibers occurs typically under the nucleus during cell locomotion.
source: Live-imaging of U2OS cells expressing Histone-H2B-mCherry to mark the nucleus, as well as LifeAct-TagGFP2 and focal adhesion marker miRFP670-paxillin, revealed that the assembly of cortical stress fibers occurred typically under the nucleus during cell locomotion (Figure 3A and Video 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to live-imaging data in Figure 3A and Video 4.

claim: ~80% of cortical stress fibers assemble underneath the nucleus.
source: Quantification of the emergence of cortical stress fibers from 19 time-lapse videos revealed that ~80% of the cortical stress fibers assembled underneath the nucleus (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to quantification data in Figure 3B.

claim: The nucleus typically consists of <30% of the cell area.
source: By considering that the nucleus typically consists of <30% of the cell area, the assembly of cortical stress fibers occurs predominantly underneath the nucleus.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as context for the quantification data.

claim: NMIIA pulses at the ventral cortex of U2OS cells are slightly more prevalent underneath the nucleus compared to the region outside the nucleus perimeter.
source: Our analysis indicated that NMIIA pulses at the ventral cortex of U2OS cells are slightly more prevalent underneath the nucleus, where cortical stress fibers also principally assembled, compared to the region outside the nucleus perimeter (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to quantification data in Figure 3C.

claim: Assembly of cortical stress fibers and enforcement of focal adhesions at their ends are associated with NMIIA pulses.
source: Interestingly, assembly of cortical stress fibers and enforcement of focal adhesions at their ends were associated with NMIIA pulses (Figure 3D and Video 7).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to imaging data in Figure 3D and Video 7.

claim: NMIIA pulses frequently coincide with F-actin bundling.
source: These experiments revealed that NMIIA pulses frequently coincided with F-actin bundling (Figure 4A and Video 8).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to three-color TIRFM data in Figure 4A and Video 8.

claim: In majority of cases the NMIIA pulses are transient and 'non-productive', and the actin filament bundles collapse back to the ventral cortex along with the cessation of the pulse.
source: In majority of cases the NMIIA pulses were transient and 'non-productive', and the actin filament bundles collapsed back to the ventral cortex along with the cessation of the pulse (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to kymograph data in Figure 4B.

claim: In some cases the NMIIA pulses are more persistent and 'productive', leading to the formation of more stable actomyosin bundles.
source: However, in some cases the NMIIA pulses were more persistent and 'productive', and led to the formation of more stable actomyosin bundles.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to imaging data in Figure 4A and C.

claim: Persistent NMIIA pulses engage paxillin positive focal adhesions, causing them to align to the direction of the pull and to increase in size.
source: These actomyosin bundles engaged paxillin positive focal adhesions, causing them to align to the direction of the pull and to increase in size, thus leading to stabilization and maturation of the cortical stress fiber (Figure 4A and C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to imaging data in Figure 4A and C.

claim: Focal adhesions associating with new cortical stress fibers can emerge de novo.
source: Importantly, focal adhesions associating with the new cortical stress fiber could either emerge de novo (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, orange arrow, Video 9) or be pre-existing adhesions that were connected to other, discrete contractile bundles (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, orange arrow and Videos 8 and 10).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to imaging data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and Video 9.

claim: Focal adhesions associating with new cortical stress fibers can be pre-existing adhesions that were connected to other, discrete contractile bundles.
source: Importantly, focal adhesions associating with the new cortical stress fiber could either emerge de novo (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, orange arrow, Video 9) or be pre-existing adhesions that were connected to other, discrete contractile bundles (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, orange arrow and Videos 8 and 10).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to imaging data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and Videos 8 and 10.

claim: One end of a cortical stress fiber can be connected to the mesh of pre-existing actomyosin bundles instead of a focal adhesion.
source: Moreover, we occasionally observed assembly of cortical stress fibers, where one end of the contractile bundle was connected to the mesh of pre-existing actomyosin bundles instead of a focal adhesion (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, yellow arrow, and Video 9).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to imaging data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and Video 9.

claim: Generation of cortical stress fibers is a very dynamic and plastic process.
source: Thus, generation of cortical stress fibers is both very dynamic and plastic process, and it can involve either de novo formation of focal adhesions or 'recycling' of pre-existing focal adhesions or higher-order actomyosin structures to connect the nascent cortical stress fiber to the cell cortex.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary of observations from imaging data.

claim: Blebbistatin does not cease myosin pulses in U2OS cells.
source: As reported earlier (Baird et al., 2017), Blebbistatin did not cease the NMII pulsatile behavior in U2OS cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Myosin pulses do not depend on the catalytic activity of NMII.
source: Thus, myosin pulses do not depend on the catalytic activity of NMII, but can occur also if the motor domain of myosin is brought to low actin-affinity state by Blebbistatin (Kovács et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation and inferred from the Blebbistatin experiments.

claim: Cortical stress fiber formation is almost completely abolished in Blebbistatin-treated cells.
source: Interestingly, the cortical stress fiber formation was almost completely abolished in Blebbistatin-treated cells, providing evidence that NMII activity is critical for the assembly of cortical stress fibers (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and Video 11).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to imaging data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and Video 11.

claim: NMII activity is critical for the assembly of cortical stress fibers.
source: Interestingly, the cortical stress fiber formation was almost completely abolished in Blebbistatin-treated cells, providing evidence that NMII activity is critical for the assembly of cortical stress fibers (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and Video 11).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Blebbistatin experiments.

claim: NMII pulses still drive transient cortical F-actin enrichment in cells devoid of integrin-based adhesions, but cannot engage F-actin bundling to the assembly of cortical stress fibers.
source: By imaging cells that had managed to adhere to the dish only from their edges, but were devoid of adhesions inside cell margins, we revealed that while NMII pulses still drove transient cortical F-actin enrichment, they could not engage F-actin bundling to the assembly of cortical stress fibers (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and Video 12).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to imaging data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and Video 12.

claim: Even after 4 hr post CK-666 administration, de novo cortical stress fiber assembly is frequently observed.
source: Even after 4 hr post drug administration, de novo cortical stress fiber assembly was frequently observed (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C and Video 13).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to imaging data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C and Video 13.

claim: NMII inhibition leads to an almost complete loss of cortical stress fibers.
source: Quantification of cortical stress fibers from control (DMSO-treated), para-amino-Blebbistatin, and CK-666 treated U2OS cells and MEFs confirmed that NMII inhibition led to an almost complete loss of cortical stress fibers, whereas Arp2/3 inhibition resulted in only a moderate decrease in the amount of these actomyosin bundles (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to quantification data in Figure 4D.

claim: Arp2/3 inhibition results in only a moderate decrease in the amount of cortical stress fibers.
source: Quantification of cortical stress fibers from control (DMSO-treated), para-amino-Blebbistatin, and CK-666 treated U2OS cells and MEFs confirmed that NMII inhibition led to an almost complete loss of cortical stress fibers, whereas Arp2/3 inhibition resulted in only a moderate decrease in the amount of these actomyosin bundles (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to quantification data in Figure 4D.

claim: Treatment of U2OS cells for 1 hr with 12.5 µM SMIFH2 decreases the amount of cortical stress fibers.
source: Treatment of U2OS cells for 1 hr with 12.5 µM SMIFH2 decreased the amount of cortical stress fibers, suggesting that formins contribute, either directly or indirectly, to the assembly of cortical stress fibers.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to quantification data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Formins contribute, either directly or indirectly, to the assembly of cortical stress fibers.
source: Treatment of U2OS cells for 1 hr with 12.5 µM SMIFH2 decreased the amount of cortical stress fibers, suggesting that formins contribute, either directly or indirectly, to the assembly of cortical stress fibers.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from SMIFH2 treatment experiments.

claim: siRNA experiments on mDia1, mDia2 and mDia3 did not result in significant reduction in the number of cortical stress fibers.
source: However, subsequent siRNA experiments on mDia1, mDia2 and mDia3, from which mDia1-2 have been linked to assembly of dorsal stress fibers and transverse arcs, did not result in significant reduction in the number of cortical stress fibers (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: mDia1-3 are either not critical for generation of cortical stress fibers or are functionally redundant with each other or with some other formins expressed in U2OS cells.
source: These results suggest that mDia1-3 are either not critical for generation of cortical stress fibers or that they are functionally redundant with each other or with some other formins expressed in U2OS cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the siRNA experiments.

claim: Generation of cortical stress fibers is driven by NMII-catalyzed reorganization of the cortical actin filament network.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that generation of cortical stress fibers is driven by NMII-catalyzed reorganization of the cortical actin filament network and dependent on integrin-based cell-matrix adhesions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Generation of cortical stress fibers is dependent on integrin-based cell-matrix adhesions.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that generation of cortical stress fibers is driven by NMII-catalyzed reorganization of the cortical actin filament network and dependent on integrin-based cell-matrix adhesions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Cortical stress fibers located at the ventral cortex of 2D-migrating cells assemble de novo through NMII-dependent reorganization of the actin cortex.
source: We show that unlike ventral stress fibers, which are generated from the pre-exiting network of dorsal stress fibers and transverse arcs (Tojkander et al., 2015), cortical stress fibers located at the ventral cortex of 2D-migrating cells assemble de novo through NMII-dependent reorganization of the actin cortex (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the main findings.

claim: Transverse arc formation does not involve prominent myosin pulses.
source: It is important to note that although generation of cortical stress fibers below the nucleus and transverse arcs at the lamellipodium–lamellum interface display some parallels, transverse arc formation does not involve prominent myosin pulses, but they are rather assembled through condensation of the lamellipodial actin filament network during the retraction phase (Burnette et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Transverse arcs are assembled through condensation of the lamellipodial actin filament network during the retraction phase.
source: It is important to note that although generation of cortical stress fibers below the nucleus and transverse arcs at the lamellipodium–lamellum interface display some parallels, transverse arc formation does not involve prominent myosin pulses, but they are rather assembled through condensation of the lamellipodial actin filament network during the retraction phase (Burnette et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Cortical stress fibers are thinner than ventral stress fibers.
source: Cortical stress fibers bear close resemblance to the ventral stress fibers because they terminate to focal adhesions at both ends, do not elongate through actin polymerization at focal adhesions, and are composed of bipolar NMII filaments and α-actinin decorated actin filaments. However, they are thinner, more dynamic, devoid of NMII stacks, and less contractile compared to ventral stress fibers.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the characteristics of cortical stress fibers.

claim: Cortical stress fibers are more dynamic than ventral stress fibers.
source: Cortical stress fibers bear close resemblance to the ventral stress fibers because they terminate to focal adhesions at both ends, do not elongate through actin polymerization at focal adhesions, and are composed of bipolar NMII filaments and α-actinin decorated actin filaments. However, they are thinner, more dynamic, devoid of NMII stacks, and less contractile compared to ventral stress fibers.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the characteristics of cortical stress fibers.

However, they are thinner, more dynamic, devoid of NMII stacks, and less contractile compared to ventral stress fibers.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the characteristics of cortical stress fibers.

claim: Cortical stress fibers terminate to focal adhesions at both ends.
source: Cortical stress fibers bear close resemblance to the ventral stress fibers because they terminate to focal adhesions at both ends, do not elongate through actin polymerization at focal adhesions, and are composed of bipolar NMII filaments and α-actinin decorated actin filaments.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the characteristics of cortical stress fibers.

evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the characteristics of cortical stress fibers.

source: Cortical stress fibers bear close resemblance to the ventral stress fibers because they terminate to focal adhesions at both ends, do not elongate through actin polymerization at focal adhesions, and are composed of bipolar NMII filaments and α-actinin decorated actin filaments.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the characteristics of cortical stress fibers.

claim: The assembly of cortical stress fibers is intimately linked to the actin cortex.
source: The assembly of cortical stress fibers is intimately linked to the actin cortex, where stochastic, NMII-mediated contractions of the cortical actin meshwork can lead to the formation of cortical actomyosin bundles.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the findings.

claim: Stochastic, NMII-mediated contractions of the cortical actin meshwork can lead to the formation of cortical actomyosin bundles.
source: The assembly of cortical stress fibers is intimately linked to the actin cortex, where stochastic, NMII-mediated contractions of the cortical actin meshwork can lead to the formation of cortical actomyosin bundles.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the findings.

claim: Cortical actomyosin bundles are initially transient by nature and can either form a cortical stress fiber or collapse back into the ventral cortex.
source: These are initially transient by nature and can either form a cortical stress fiber or collapse back into the ventral cortex.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the findings.

claim: Transient NMII pulse-driven cortical actin condensations drive tissue morphogenesis in epithelial tissues of developing organisms.
source: Although NMII-pulses have not been previously linked to assembly of contractile actomyosin bundles, transient NMII pulse-driven cortical actin condensations were reported to occur in epithelial tissues of developing organisms where they drive tissue morphogenesis (Munro et al., 2004; Solon et al., 2009; Rauzi et al., 2010; Munjal et al., 2015; Michaux et al., 2018) and in cells of mesenchymal origin migrating in 2D environment (Kim and Davidson, 2011; Nie et al., 2015; Baird et al., 2017; Graessl et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Transient NMII pulse-driven cortical actin condensations occur in cells of mesenchymal origin migrating in 2D environment.
source: Although NMII-pulses have not been previously linked to assembly of contractile actomyosin bundles, transient NMII pulse-driven cortical actin condensations were reported to occur in epithelial tissues of developing organisms where they drive tissue morphogenesis (Munro et al., 2004; Solon et al., 2009; Rauzi et al., 2010; Munjal et al., 2015; Michaux et al., 2018) and in cells of mesenchymal origin migrating in 2D environment (Kim and Davidson, 2011; Nie et al., 2015; Baird et al., 2017; Graessl et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: In Drosophila epithelia, NMII/actin foci undergo E-cadherin-mediated stabilization into medioapical filaments.
source: In Drosophila epithelia, the NMII/actin foci were also reported to undergo E-cadherin-mediated stabilization into medioapical filaments (Mason et al., 2013; Vasquez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Myosin II pulse-driven F-actin bundling may have a more general role in the formation of different types of contractile actomyosin bundles in cells.
source: Thus, myosin II pulse-driven F-actin bundling may have a more general role in the formation of different types of contractile actomyosin bundles in cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as speculation based on the findings and literature.

claim: During cytokinesis, small actomyosin nodes can coalescence and form highly ordered contractile bundles at the cleavage furrow.
source: Also during cytokinesis, small actomyosin nodes can coalescence and form highly ordered contractile bundles at the cleavage furrow (Laplante et al., 2016; Reymann et al., 2016; Henson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Initially very similar cortical actomyosin foci appear to drive the formation of various different contractile structures.
source: Thus, initially very similar cortical actomyosin foci appear drive the formation of various different contractile structures.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from the findings and literature.

claim: Nascent cortical stress fibers come in many intermediate shapes that reflect the initially random formation of NMII/F-actin clusters.
source: Similarly, the nascent cortical stress fibers come in many intermediate shapes that reflect the initially random formation of NMII/F-actin clusters.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on observations from imaging data.

claim: During cortical stress fiber assembly, intermediate structures can become momentarily engaged by more than two focal adhesions, but usually two focal adhesions become dominant at the ends.
source: These intermediate structures can become momentarily engaged by more than two focal adhesions, but during subsequent tug-of-war-type process usually two focal adhesions become dominant at the ends of the cortical stress fiber.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on observations from imaging data.

claim: New actomyosin bundles can emerge from the actin cortex close to a pre-existing stress fiber and exhibit a mechanical continuum with the actomyosin cortex.
source: Moreover, a recent study reported emergence of new actomyosin bundles from the actin cortex close to a pre-existing stress fiber, and demonstrated that these actomyosin bundles exhibit a mechanical continuum with the actomyosin cortex (Vignaud et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: The degree of cortical F-actin network bundling may be dependent on both the mesh gap-size and thickness of the actin meshwork that vary between different cell types.
source: The degree of cortical F-actin network bundling may be dependent on both the mesh gap-size and thickness of the actin meshwork that vary between different cell types (Bovellan et al., 2014; Svitkina, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: The actin cortex appears to be more dense and under higher tension at the back of 2D-migrating cells.
source: Interestingly, the actin cortex appears to be more dense and under higher tension at the back of the 2D-migrating cells (Chugh and Paluch, 2018; Bisaria et al., 2020), where we observe the most prominent cortical stress fiber assembly.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Transportation of the nucleus in cells migrating in tissue environment poses mechanical challenges, especially when facing narrow passages.
source: Transportation of the relatively rigid nucleus in cells migrating in tissue environment poses mechanical challenges, especially when facing narrow passages (Petrie et al., 2014; Denais et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Contractile F-actin bundles accumulate around the nucleus to mediate movement of the nucleus through constrictions.
source: This results in accumulation of contractile F-actin bundles around the nucleus to mediate movement of the nucleus through the constriction (Thomas et al., 2015; Davidson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: When MEF or U2OS cells adhere and migrate along narrow ECM-coated tracks, directional F-actin bundles are observed under the nucleus.
source: Similarly, when subjecting MEF or U2OS cells to adhere and migrate along narrow ECM-coated tracks, directional F-actin bundles are observed under the nucleus (Doyle et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Stress fibers underneath the nucleus appear to be largely independent of LINC-complex.
source: The stress fibers underneath the nucleus appear to be largely independent of linker of nucleus and cytoskeleton (LINC)-complex, which is known to mediate contacts between the nuclear envelope and perinuclear cap fibers at the dorsal surface of the nucleus (Luxton et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2014; Calero-Cuenca et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: RhoA pulses upstream of NMII localize mainly near the cell center.
source: Interestingly, RhoA pulses upstream of NMII were also found to localize mainly near the cell center (Graessl et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: It would be difficult to generate stress fibers protecting the nucleus from the transverse arc network in cells migrating in 3D environment.
source: Although the mechanisms by which these actomyosin bundles protecting the nucleus are assembled is still unknown, we envision that it would be difficult to generate such fibers from the transverse arc network, which to our knowledge is not generally present in cells migrating in a 3D environment (Doyle et al., 2015; Thomas et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations as speculation.

claim: The de novo mechanism to generate cortical stress fibers is well suited for generation of stress fibers in 3D environment to protect the nucleus during migration.
source: Thus, the de novo mechanism to generate contractile cortical stress fibers reported here is well suited for generation of stress fibers in 3D environment to protect the nucleus during migration.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as speculation based on the findings.

claim: Cells in 3D environment utilizing mesenchymal migration mode exhibit multiple focal adhesion-mediated ECM attachments around their dorso-ventral and antero-posterior axis.
source: In line with this hypothesis, cells in 3D environment utilizing mesenchymal migration mode exhibit multiple focal adhesion-mediated ECM attachments around their dorso-ventral and antero-posterior axis, and impose greater challenges with protecting the integrity of the nucleus than cells in 2D (Yamada and Sixt, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: U2OS cells migrating in 3D fibrin network exhibit short, adhesion-attached actomyosin bundles close to nuclei.
source: We indeed observed short, adhesion-attached actomyosin bundles close to nuclei in U2OS cells migrating in 3D fibrin network.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to imaging data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Myosin II pulse-induced actin contractions are linked to maturation of nascent focal adhesions at the cell cortex.
source: Taken together, we demonstrate that the myosin II pulse-induced actin contractions are linked to maturation of nascent focal adhesions at the cell cortex, and this can lead to an assembly of a contractile stress fiber that is attached to focal adhesions at its both ends.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the findings.

claim: The new mechanism for stress fiber assembly allows assembly of stress fibers in conditions where pre-existing stress fiber precursors are not present.
source: This new mechanism expands the toolbox that cells can apply for generation of stress fibers, thus allowing assembly of stress fibers also in conditions where the pre-existing stress fiber precursors (transverse arcs and dorsal stress fibers) are not present.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the implications of the findings.

claim: U2OS cells were obtained from ATCC.
source: Wild-type MEFs (a gift from J.Eriksson's lab) and U2OS (ATCC HTB-96, verified through STR profiling) cells were cultured in high-glucose DMEM (Lonza, BE12-119F), supplemented with 10% FBS (Gibco, 10500–064), 10 U/ml penicillin, 10 µg/ml streptomycin, and 20 mM L-glutamine (Gibco, 10378–016) (from here on referred as complete DMEM) and kept at +37°C in a humidified atmosphere with 5% CO2.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: U2OS cells were verified through STR profiling.
source: Wild-type MEFs (a gift from J.Eriksson's lab) and U2OS (ATCC HTB-96, verified through STR profiling) cells were cultured in high-glucose DMEM (Lonza, BE12-119F), supplemented with 10% FBS (Gibco, 10500–064), 10 U/ml penicillin, 10 µg/ml streptomycin, and 20 mM L-glutamine (Gibco, 10378–016) (from here on referred as complete DMEM) and kept at +37°C in a humidified atmosphere with 5% CO2.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: 3D-SIM images were obtained using Deltavision OMX SR with 60×/1.42NA PlanApo N oil objective.
source: All 3D-SIM images were obtained at RT, using Deltavision OMX SR (Cytiva) with 60×/1.42NA PlanApo N oil objective with 1.516 RI immersion oil, a laser module with 405-, 488-, 568-, and 640 nm diode laser lines and three sCMOS cameras, operated through Acquire SR 4.4 acquisition software.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Live-cell TIRF experiments used Ring-TIRF module from Deltavision OMX SR with 60×/1.49NA Apo N oil objective.
source: For live-cell TIRF experiments, the Ring-TIRF module from the Deltavision OMX SR (Cytiva) with 60×/1.49NA Apo N oil objective (Olympus), 1.522 RI immersion oil and imaging chamber with controlled humidified atmosphere of 5% CO2 and 37°C was utilized.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Traction force microscopy experiments used polyacrylamide gels with Young's Modulus of 26 kPa.
source: Next day, cells were re-plated on polyacrylamide (PAA) gels of known stiffness (Young's Modulus/elastic modulus = 26 kPa) coated with mixture of collagen and fibronectin and incubated for 2–4 hr prior to imaging.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.
